title: Discourse Obligations in Dialogue Processing
abstract: Models discourse obligations as dialogue attitudes that persist in conversational context, including obligations created by questions and other dialogue acts, providing a precursor to longitudinal commitment tracking.
venue: 32nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics

admission.reason: The abstract establishes persistent discourse obligations created by dialogue acts, but it does not show mechanisms or evaluation for modifying, retracting, superseding, reopening, or resolving those obligations across successive communications. The terminology is adjacent to F7, but the capability does not materially strengthen the unresolved revision problem.

title: Investigating Reasons for Disagreement in Natural Language Inference
abstract: Develops a taxonomy of sources of disagreement in natural-language inference and evaluates modeling approaches that retain multiple possible labels when evidence or interpretation does not warrant a single resolved judgment.
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics

admission.reason: The paper studies why annotators disagree on generic NLI judgments and how to preserve multiple labels. That is useful for ambiguity modeling, but the abstract does not maintain a longitudinal evidence-backed work-item state or distinguish revision relations over successive assertions. Under this Topic's exclusions, generic NLI disagreement alone is insufficient.

title: Inherent Disagreements in Human Textual Inferences
abstract: Shows that disagreement about natural-language inference often persists rather than disappearing as annotation noise and argues that models should preserve distributions of plausible judgments rather than force a single interpretation.
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics

admission.reason: The abstract shows that some NLI disagreements are inherently plural and should not always be collapsed to one label, but it does not track a work item through time, relate later assertions to earlier ones, or retain evidence-backed lifecycle states. It is a generic inference-ambiguity result rather than a longitudinal state-resolution method.

title: On the logic of theory change: Partial meet contraction and revision functions
abstract: Develops formal postulates and representation results for contraction and revision of belief theories, including partial-meet contraction, providing foundational machinery for distinguishing belief revision from simple addition or deletion.

admission.reason: Partial-meet contraction and revision is foundational belief-revision theory, but the stated corpus already contains formal treatments of revision and retraction. This abstract does not add an empirical natural-language method, provenance-preserving implementation, or operational-communication evaluation needed by the remaining gaps. It therefore duplicates an already-covered formal capability rather than materially advancing the open problem.

title: User Edits Classification Using Document Revision Histories
abstract: Uses document revision histories to distinguish factual edits from fluency edits, demonstrating that revision sequences can be classified according to the semantic significance of changes rather than only their lexical form.

admission.reason: The paper distinguishes factual edits from fluency edits in revision histories, but the abstract does not expose revision relations such as correction, supersession, supplementation, contradiction, reopening, or unresolved conflict. Re3 provides a broader aligned revision/action/intent representation, so this weaker UNCHECKED candidate does not justify an additional reading slot.

title: Operational specification of a commitment-based agent communication language
abstract: Defines agent communication semantics through social commitments, including conditional commitments and precommitments, and specifies how communicative acts operate on commitment objects as interactions evolve.

admission.reason: The abstract provides formal semantics for conditional commitments and precommitments, but the current gaps already acknowledge formal commitment models and instead require natural-language longitudinal revision and workplace evidence. It does not explicitly demonstrate cancellation, revocation, reopening, contradiction resolution, or evaluated language understanding over successive operational messages.

title: A Consensus Glossary of Temporal Database Concepts
abstract: Defines and systematizes temporal-database concepts including distinctions needed to represent facts whose validity and database history vary over time, providing terminology relevant to valid-time versus observation or transaction-time reasoning.

admission.reason: The temporal-database glossary supplies terminology for valid and transaction time, but the remaining gap is an evaluated multi-time representation for the product's state-resolution task. A terminology consensus document does not materially advance that evaluation, and the gap statement already records related temporal-database formal coverage.

title: One Document, Many Revisions: A Dataset for Classification and Description of Edit Intents
abstract: Provides full Wikipedia revision histories annotated for edit intent and studies both classification of revision purposes and generation of free-form descriptions of changes across document versions.

admission.reason: Full revision histories and edit-intent labels are relevant to F12, but the abstract still classifies purposes of edits rather than semantic relations between competing assertions. Re3 is the stronger candidate because it additionally aligns revisions with reviews and author responses. With identity UNCHECKED and overlapping capability, this candidate does not justify another reading slot.

title: Identifying Semantic Edit Intentions from Revisions in Wikipedia
abstract: Introduces a taxonomy of semantic intentions behind Wikipedia edits and trains a classifier to infer those intentions from revision data, moving beyond purely syntactic edit operations.

admission.reason: The paper classifies semantic intentions behind Wikipedia edits, but the abstract does not establish that its taxonomy distinguishes the relations required here: correction, retraction, supersession, supplementation, contradiction, reopening, and unresolved conflict. The shared word 'semantic' is insufficient to show the needed revision capability.

title: Using Context to Predict the Purpose of Argumentative Writing Revisions
abstract: Predicts the purpose of revisions in argumentative writing using contextual information, contributing methods for classifying why a textual revision was made rather than merely detecting its surface change.

admission.reason: Predicting why argumentative-writing revisions were made is adjacent to F12, but the abstract does not model the truth status of earlier versus later assertions, lifecycle transitions, or the required revision-relation inventory. Its capability is revision-purpose classification rather than longitudinal state resolution.

title: Automatically Classifying Edit Categories in Wikipedia Revisions
abstract: Develops automatic classification of Wikipedia revision edits into categories, providing empirical machinery for assigning semantic or functional meaning to changes across document versions.

admission.reason: Automatic edit-category classification in Wikipedia is too generic for the target. The abstract does not show semantic lineage between assertions or distinguish correction, supersession, contradiction, reopening, and unresolved conflict. Stronger revision candidates are available, so this UNCHECKED paper would mainly duplicate background capability.

title: Temporal Interpretation, Discourse Relations, and Commonsense Entailment
abstract: Provides a formal account of discourse relations and temporal relations between events using defeasible rules and commonsense knowledge, showing how similar surface forms can receive different temporal and discourse interpretations.

admission.reason: The formal treatment of temporal interpretation and discourse relations is relevant background, but the abstract does not provide an evaluated extraction or longitudinal state-tracking method. More directly usable temporal candidates in this round include joint timeline inference and temporal parsing, so this theoretical paper does not materially strengthen the current evidence base.

title: Provenance in Databases: Why, How, and Where
abstract: Surveys why-, how-, and where-provenance for database queries and their applications to confidence, updates, debugging, and annotation propagation, providing foundations for retaining derivational lineage rather than only current values.

admission.reason: Why-, how-, and where-provenance are foundational for lineage, but this is a broad database-provenance survey rather than an evaluated temporal state-resolution method. Gap 8 specifically requires benchmarking a provenance-preserving implementation for immutable observations, successive assessments, and a derived current-state view; the abstract does not establish that capability.

title: Jointly Combining Implicit Constraints Improves Temporal Ordering
abstract: Shows that temporal-relation predictions can be improved by joint inference that enforces implicit consistency constraints among relations instead of classifying each event pair independently.

admission.reason: Global consistency constraints for temporal ordering are relevant to F4, but the capability substantially overlaps the admitted joint event-timeline candidate, which additionally integrates interval representations and event coreference. With identity UNCHECKED and no longitudinal workplace or revision component, this paper does not add enough distinct value for another slot.

title: TimeML: Robust Specification of Event and Temporal Expressions in Text
abstract: Defines TimeML for annotating events, temporal expressions, event-time anchoring, and temporal ordering across sentences and discourse, including underspecified temporal interpretations and modal contexts.
venue: AAAI Spring Symposium: New Directions in Question Answering

admission.reason: TimeML is foundational for event and temporal-expression annotation, but the current corpus already has temporal extraction and reasoning coverage and the unresolved gaps concern longitudinal combination, multi-time product evaluation, and revision semantics. The abstract defines an annotation specification rather than adding a new evaluated state-resolution capability. Identity is also UNCHECKED.

title: Neural Ranking Models for Temporal Dependency Structure Parsing
abstract: Builds a neural temporal dependency parser that organizes textual events and time expressions into a temporal dependency tree and evaluates it on both news and narrative domains.

admission.reason: The verified paper provides evaluated temporal dependency parsing across news and narrative domains, but this is still a standard temporal-structure component rather than longitudinal work-item revision or multi-time state resolution. The admitted joint timeline paper contributes the more directly needed global-consistency capability, so this otherwise relevant paper is redundant for this round.
